author: ch402
text:
It increasingly seems to me that the next big barrier in mechanistic interpretability will be an engineering one.

If you are an engineer who wants to help us scale up this work, please consider applying! Your support could really accelerate interpretability right now.

quoted.text:
If you'd asked me a year ago, superposition would have been by far the reason I was most worried that mechanistic interpretability would hit a dead end.

I'm now very optimistic. I'd go as far as saying it's now primarily an engineering problem -- hard, but less fundamental risk.

quoted.text: The fact that most individual neurons are uninterpretable presents a serious roadblock to a mechanistic understanding of language models. We demonstrate a method for decomposing groups of neurons into interpretable features with the potential to move past that roadblock.

author: ch402

I think of mechanistic interpretability as aiming to be a "microscopic theory" of machine learning, in contrast to scaling laws as a "macroscopic theory".

The fact that induction heads can explain certain exceptions to general macroscopic trends seem like a healthy sign. https://t.co/RgFQk1nFEQ

This thread expresses one way of thinking about all of this…

But the thing I'd really encourage you to ask is what you believe, and where you're uncertain. The discourse often focuses on very specific views, when there are so many dimensions on which one might be uncertain. https://t.co/uzaz6RPhYh

author: ch402
text:
A concrete "easy scenario":  LLMs are just straightforwardly generative models over possible writers, and RLHF just selects within that space. We can then select for brilliant, knowledgeable, kind, thoughtful experts on any topic.

I wouldn't bet on this, but it's possible!

author: ch402
text:
There's a lot of debate about what values AI systems should be trained to have.

I'm excited about Constitutional AI making this more legible by training models to follow a human readable constitution.

quoted.text: We’ve now published a post describing the Constitutional AI approach, as well as the constitution we’ve used to train Claude: https://t.co/eLtcqG7MuQ

author: ch402
text: It also suggests that studying the mechanisms which develop in artificial neural networks may teach much more general lessons -- that lessons from artificial neural nets might possibly transfer to biological systems!

author: ch402
text:
@BartenOtto Some things that seem different between traditional engineering teams and research teams (although of course lots of room in between):

- Engineering teams often know the end goal and intervening steps, which allows project planning. Research teams don't.

author: ch402
text:
It's surprisingly how little there is on "how to run a research group."

Lots of great resources on being a researcher (eg. You and Your Research), and on leading other types of teams (eg. books on software engineering management). Research leadership seems like an open problem.

author: ch402
text: Something this thread is implicitly getting at is that there's a trade-off between helpfulness and harmlessness. I think the pareto frontier perspective is very helpful here: https://t.co/V0kUA118Es

quoted.text: In our paper, we describe how we’ve used Constitutional AI to train better and more harmless AI assistants without any human feedback labels for harms. This approach leads to models that are safer and also more helpful. https://t.co/PXvWk3fz0o

author: ch402
text: I'm pretty excited about this as a step towards a mechanistic theory of memorization and overfitting.

quoted.text:
We have little mechanistic understanding of how deep learning models overfit to their training data, despite it being a central problem. Here we extend our previous work on toy models to shed light on how models generalize beyond their training data.
https://t.co/0bYUToop3m https://t.co/88KGnM3CsL

author: ch402
text: An idea I've been toying with: The role of many toy models may be to serve as "counterexamples in mechanistic interpretability".

quoted.text: Great question! In all honesty, we just don't really know. I consider this an open scientific question, and really want to get more data on it! Some thoughts: 🧵
